description.summary: Ghosts are alleged manifestations of the dead — visual apparitions, voices, sounds, and physical effects — reported across virtually every human culture from Mesopotamia to the present. Mainstream science treats them as folklore and misperception; parapsychology and Spiritualism continue to study them as a possible class of phenomena.
description.full: A ghost is the alleged spirit, soul, or image of a dead person manifesting to the living. The belief is one of the oldest and most cross-cultural in human history, attested in Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Greek, Roman, Chinese, Japanese, Indian, and many Indigenous traditions, and continuing through medieval Christendom, the Renaissance, and the modern era. Common features of ghost reports include visual apparitions (full-body, partial, or 'misty'), disembodied voices and sounds, cold spots, object movement, electromagnetic anomalies, and a sense of presence or being watched. Hauntings are commonly classified as 'intelligent' (apparently aware and interactive) or 'residual' (repeating, non-interactive recordings of past events). The Spiritualist movement in the United States and Britain — usually dated from the Hydesville rappings reported by the Fox sisters in 1848 — produced an enormous public engagement with mediumship and ghosts, and led directly to the founding of the (British) Society for Psychical Research in 1882, the American SPR in 1885, and the academic discipline of parapsychology. Famous modern cases include the Borley Rectory investigations by Harry Price (1929–1939), the Enfield poltergeist investigated by Maurice Grosse and Guy Lyon Playfair (1977–1979), and the Rosenheim poltergeist studied by Hans Bender (1967). Mainstream scientific consensus treats ghosts as a non-existent phenomenon explicable by perceptual error, sleep paralysis, infrasound, electromagnetic fields, hoaxing, and cultural expectation; the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry and individual investigators such as Joe Nickell and Benjamin Radford are leading skeptical voices. Despite this, polling consistently shows that a substantial minority of adults in many countries report personal ghost experiences.

etymology.origin: English 'ghost' from Old English gāst ('breath, spirit'), from Proto-Germanic *gaistaz. Cognate with German Geist.
etymology.meaning: Originally 'breath' or 'soul'; came to mean 'spirit of the dead' through Christian usage.

features.description: Full-body, partial, or misty figures, often dressed in period clothing
Voices, footsteps, music, knocks, raps without identifiable source
Localized drops in temperature commonly reported during alleged hauntings
Items moving, falling, or being thrown — characteristic of poltergeist cases
Reported fluctuations on EMF meters, lights flickering, electronic interference
Feeling watched or accompanied without visible cause
Reports of being touched, pushed, or held

physical.morphology: Reports range from translucent or 'misty' figures, through full-bodied apparitions indistinguishable from the living, to entirely non-visual phenomena (sounds, sensations, electromagnetic effects).

abilities.description: Appearing as a visible figure or partial image
Producing sounds — voices, footsteps, knocking, music
Moving or affecting physical objects (poltergeist activity)
Reportedly communicating through mediums, Ouija boards, EVP, and direct apparition
Tied to specific locations associated with the deceased — 'haunting' in the strict sense

habitat_preference: battlefields and sites of violent death
places of long human occupation (castles, prisons, hospitals, theatres)
patterns: Often tied to a specific location ('haunting')
Reports cluster around anniversaries of death or significant events
Activity frequently reported at night, in low-stimulus settings
'Intelligent' hauntings interact with witnesses; 'residual' hauntings repeat without acknowledgment

range.description: Ghost beliefs are virtually universal across human cultures, attested from at least the third millennium BC (Mesopotamian texts) to the present. Reports occur worldwide; concentrations of widely-publicized cases exist in the British Isles, the United States, Japan, China, and Latin America.

temporal.seasonal_patterns: In many cultures, ghosts are most associated with autumn / winter festivals of the dead — Samhain / Halloween (31 October–1 November), the Mexican Día de los Muertos (1–2 November), the Chinese Hungry Ghost Festival (7th lunar month), the Japanese Obon (mid-August), and the Christian All Souls' Day (2 November).

origins.cultural_roots: Belief in ghosts is documented in Mesopotamian (Akkadian etemmu), Egyptian (akh, ka), Greek (eidolon, psyche), Roman (manes, lemures), Chinese (gui), Indian (bhoota, pret), and many Indigenous traditions. The dead are typically expected to require ritual care (burial, offerings, prayers); failure to provide it produces unquiet ghosts.
origins.earliest_accounts: Mesopotamian incantation and funerary texts (3rd–1st millennium BC) refer to ghosts (etemmu) of the dead. Homer's Odyssey (8th century BC) describes the shades in the underworld. Pliny the Younger (c. 50 BC – 113 AD) recounts Athenodorus's encounter with a chained ghost in Athens, often cited as the first Western 'haunted house' narrative.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to wider afterlife traditions: heaven and hell, purgatory, ancestor worship, spiritualism, and necromancy.

history.modern_era: From the 1990s onward, ghost reports have been mediated by reality-TV ghost-hunting programmes (Most Haunted, Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures), online sighting databases, and digital evidence (EVP recordings, IR/thermal video). Mainstream science continues to treat ghosts as folklore explained by perception, suggestion, environmental factors, and hoaxing; parapsychology persists as a small academic discipline.

photographic.name: Spiritualist-era spirit photographs
photographic.description: A genre of 19th and early 20th century photographs purporting to show spirits alongside living sitters; produced commercially by figures including William H. Mumler (Boston, 1862) and William Hope (Crewe Circle, 1900s–1920s).
photographic.analysis: Most prominent examples were exposed as double-exposure or compositing techniques; Mumler tried for fraud in 1869, Hope investigated and exposed by Harry Price in 1922.

audio.name: Electronic voice phenomena (EVP)
audio.description: Audio recordings, beginning with the work of Friedrich Jürgenson (1959) and Konstantin Raudive (1971), interpreted as voices of the dead embedded in tape or digital noise.
audio.analysis: Mainstream explanation: pareidolia (auditory pattern-matching), radio bleed-through, and microphone artefacts. Investigated by parapsychologists and skeptics including Joe Nickell.

documentary.name: Society for Psychical Research case archives
documentary.description: Systematic case collections including 'Phantasms of the Living' (Gurney, Myers and Podmore, 1886) and the 'Census of Hallucinations' (Sidgwick et al., 1894).
documentary.analysis: Most influential corpus of historical apparition cases; methodology debated by both believers and skeptics.

paranormal.name: Spirits of the dead (animism / Spiritualism)
paranormal.description: Ghosts are the surviving consciousness or soul of a dead person, sometimes able to interact with the living.

paranormal.name: Stone tape / residual recording
paranormal.description: Hauntings are environmental 'recordings' of past events imprinted in materials (especially stone), played back under suitable conditions; the 'ghost' is not a conscious entity.
proponents: Peter Sasdy (1972 BBC play 'The Stone Tape')
evidence_cited: Repetitive, non-interactive apparitions tied to specific places

paranormal.name: Crisis apparition / telepathic projection
paranormal.description: Apparitions of a person at or near the moment of death, interpreted as a telepathic communication received by the witness.
evidence_cited: Gurney, Myers & Podmore, Phantasms of the Living (1886) — 702 cases

skeptical.name: Perceptual error and hallucination
skeptical.description: Ghost reports are explained by ordinary perceptual phenomena: pareidolia (face-pattern matching), peripheral-vision misperception, hypnagogic and hypnopompic imagery, and sleep paralysis.
evidence_cited: High prevalence of sleep paralysis in 'visit at the bedside' reports

skeptical.name: Environmental factors (infrasound, EMF, CO)
skeptical.description: Some hauntings are explicable by infrasound (Vic Tandy, 1998), strong electromagnetic fields stimulating the temporal lobe (Michael Persinger), or carbon monoxide poisoning altering perception.
evidence_cited: Tandy, V. (1998), 'The ghost in the machine'

skeptical.name: Hoax, suggestion, and cultural transmission
skeptical.description: A substantial fraction of high-profile cases involve deliberate hoaxing or social-contagion expectation effects amplified by media.
evidence_cited: Mumler and Hope spirit-photography fraud cases
Janet Hodgson's later admissions in the Enfield case

folklore.beliefs: Ghost beliefs are near-universal across cultures, varying widely in their theological framing. Common motifs include the importance of proper funerary rites, the special danger of the violent or untimely dead, and protective practices (light, salt, threshold rituals, prayer).
